problem: Existing language grounding modules for embodied agents (vector concatenation, gated networks like FiLM, convolutional interaction) modulate visual features in a fixed feature space and have limited expressiveness, so they struggle with partial observability, cluttered visuals and large command spaces.
motivation: Language grounding is the core of the perception system for language-directed navigation agents trained end-to-end by RL from sparse rewards. A more expressive yet simple grounding module could improve navigation without task-specific structural biases and could be plugged into other vision-language architectures.
key_idea: Treat latent sentence embeddings as command-dependent transformation matrices (reshaped into D x (D+1) matrices) that are applied sequentially to a CNN feature cube (Guided Feature Transformation, GFT).
insight: Each GFT step performs a language-guided rotate-scale-rotate of the feature space (SVD view), which generalizes FiLM/gated networks (recovered when U, V are identities) and acts as multi-step concept detection with language-dependent 1x1 filters. Results show GFT-1 already beats FiLM strongly in 3D (e.g. nav_near 78.3 vs 68.0), and GFT-2 gives a further jump in 2D where visual variance is high, supporting the claim that rotating the feature space per command relieves pressure on the visual features. J=3 saturates.
method: GFT module: CNN produces feature cube C (D x N); the sentence embedding yields J matrices T_j (D x (D+1)); C^[j]=g(T_j [C^[j-1]; 1^T]) with ReLU g, output C^[J] is the grounding result.
Theoretical unification: SVD of T' shows GFT is a stack of generalized gated networks (FiLM when U,V=I) and equals multi-step 1x1 convolutional concept detection.
T_j generation: bag-of-words sum-pooled 128-d word embeddings passed through a two-layer MLP (128 -> 4160 units for D=64); GFT-2 shares first MLP layer between T_1 and T_2.
Agent architecture: three-layer CNN, then GFT, then GRU for visual history, GRU for action history, GRU fusing them; shared policy/value MLP heads.
Training: ParallelA2C (32 agents, batch 128, RMSprop lr 1e-5, gamma 0.99, entropy 0.05) for 2M batches from scratch with sparse rewards (+1/-1, -0.01 per step) and a curriculum of map sizes 3-8.
XWorld3D environment: released 3D environment with teacher infrastructure for customizing commands, maps and curricula; five task types (nav, nav_nr, nav_bw, nav_avoid, nav_dir).

setting.backbone: 3-layer CNN + GFT + GRUs, trained from scratch with A2C
setting.training_data: RL from scratch in XWorld2D/XWorld3D self-generated sessions (2M minibatches, curriculum); no pretrained CNN, parser or auxiliary tasks
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (80x80 in 2D, 84x84 in 3D) with partial observability plus a text command
setting.action_space: discrete: move forward/backward/left/right, turn left/right (90 deg in 2D, 45 deg in 3D)

numbers.eval_set_note: 10k test sessions on 8x8 maps, averaged over 4 seeds x last 3 passes

numbers_note: Custom benchmarks (XWorld2D/3D), not standard VLN benchmarks; generalization tables on 9x9, 10x10, 11x11 maps in appendix not listed. Success rates only; no SPL.
results: GFT-2 achieves the best success in all five 2D task types (e.g. nav 70.7 vs best baseline Concept 64.6) and clearly beats FiLM in 3D (GFT-1 nav_near 78.3 vs FiLM 68.0; nav_dir over 15% gain). Advantages persist on larger unseen maps (9x9-11x11).
limitations: GFT needs a large projection matrix (128x4160 for D=64) and parameters grow linearly with J, so it has more parameters than FiLM.
More transformation steps make it slower than single-step gated networks.
Evaluated only on synthetic simple-grammar navigation with BoW command encoding; nav_dir in 3D remains hard (~61%) due to perspective distortion.
